strengths: The paper is clearly written, and the core idea—reward-guided detection of reward plateaus followed by inversion with adaptively increasing rollback depth—is intuitive, easy to implement, and plausibly model-agnostic. Algorithm 1 and Figure 1 make the method reproducible in principle.

The evaluation covers two standard text-to-image benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench), four human-aligned metrics, and reasonable ablations over reward model choice, accept threshold, search depth, and exploration initiation criteria, including an informative quality-vs-NFE trade-off analysis (Always vs. Random vs. Reward-Based).

The method targets a practical concern (test-time compute efficiency): reported gains are achieved at ~7.6x NFEs versus ~10x for SOP, and ablations show sensible scaling behavior with deeper/more permissive exploration.
The paper is honest that IR gains partly reflect the reward model's role in shaping the search, and acknowledges that combining reward models is left to future work.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially SDEdit-style re-noising (the 'inversion' in Eq. (5) injects fresh random noise rather than a deterministic DDIM inversion) combined with a greedy reward-acceptance loop with increasing rollback depth. This is an incremental combination of existing ingredients (Restart Sampling, RePaint resampling, Z-Sampling, SOP/evolutionary search) with an adaptive depth schedule; the hill-climbing framing is a heuristic analogy rather than an analysis, with no formal or empirical characterization of the 'local maxima' being escaped.

Evaluation is potentially biased: ImageReward is both the reward model driving the search and the primary reported metric, and its margin over SOP (0.776 vs. 0.677) is the largest gain, while gains on independent metrics are very small (e.g., HPS v2: 0.2678 vs. 0.2671; PickScore: 20.913 vs. 20.896 on Pick-a-Pic). No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or human evaluation are provided to establish that these margins are meaningful.

Generality claims are under-supported. Despite claiming the method is 'model-agnostic' and broadly applicable, all experiments use a single model (SD 2.1-base); there are no results on other diffusion backbones, video, or other conditional tasks. The justification for restricting exploration to the first λ steps is empirical and hand-wavy ('above 0.02 weight').

Baselines are matched only loosely (SOP with 5 candidates 'to ensure comparable NFEs'); a compute-matched quality/NFE trade-off curve against SOP and other test-time scaling methods, rather than a single operating point, would be needed to substantiate the efficiency advantage. Notably, the paper's own 'Always' ablation outperforms the main configuration on IR (0.931 vs. 0.776), complicating the claim that reward-based triggering offers the best practical trade-off.

The exploratory random noise in Eq. (5) blurs the line with simply restarting from a noisier state (SDEdit / Restart Sampling); the paper does not empirically isolate the contribution of adaptive depth versus this simpler baseline, and a straightforward SDEdit-style ablation is missing.

Several design details are underspecified or internally inconsistent: 'search depth is unbounded' yet 'the total candidate budget N per inversion step guarantees termination' is not justified; the batched Nb strategy interacts with δ in ways described only qualitatively; and no code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many hyperparameters (λ, δ, N, Nb, dmax).
No discussion of reward-hacking risks (over-optimization toward ImageReward), failure modes, or limitations section, which is a notable omission for a test-time alignment method.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, and the core idea—reward-guided detection of stagnation followed by adaptively deeper noise inversion—is intuitive and well motivated. The comparison of Resampling, Z-Sampling, Path Search, and Ctrl-Z in Figure 1 and the Methods section effectively positions the method.
The method is model-agnostic and requires no training, and the algorithm (Algorithm 1) is specified in enough detail to be reproducible in principle.
The ablation studies cover the main design axes (reward model choice, initiation criterion, max inversion depth, accept threshold), which is more thorough than many papers in this space.
The efficiency framing (quality vs. NFE trade-off, e.g., Always vs. Random vs. Reward-Based initiation) is a practical contribution, even if the results complicate the paper's own narrative.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and incremental contribution. The method is a fairly small modification of existing reward-guided backward/rollback sampling strategies (RePaint resampling, Z-Sampling, SOP, and other test-time scaling works such as He et al. 2025 and Zhang et al. 2025). The main new ingredient is progressively increasing the rollback depth when local perturbations fail—an adaptive search heuristic rather than a conceptual advance. The paper itself concedes SOP is the closest baseline and the advantage is a modest NFE reduction.

Evidence of reward over-optimization undermines the headline claim. The largest reported gains are on ImageReward, which is also the reward model steering the search; gains on the CLIP-based alignment metrics (HPSv2: 0.2678 vs. 0.2671 for SOP on Pick-a-Pic; PickScore +0.017) are marginal. This pattern is consistent with the sampler gaming its own reward rather than genuinely improving alignment or quality, and no human evaluation is provided to rule this out.

The ablations weaken the paper's central design claim. In Table 2, the 'Always explore' baseline outperforms the proposed reward-based stagnation detection on most metrics (e.g., IR 0.931 vs. 0.656 on Pick-a-Pic; HPSv2 0.2690 vs. 0.2646). This suggests the detection mechanism—the core novelty—may be primarily a cost-saving heuristic rather than a quality-improving mechanism, which is a substantive problem for the framing of the contribution.

Experimental scope is narrow. Only one diffusion model (Stable Diffusion 2.1) and two prompt sets are evaluated. For a method claimed to be 'broadly applicable' and 'model-agnostic', results on at least one modern architecture (SDXL, FLUX) or another modality would be expected; there is no evidence the approach transfers.

Computational cost accounting is incomplete. The reported 7.6× NFE figure counts diffusion function evaluations, but the method requires an additional reward-model forward pass at every step and for every candidate; the actual wall-clock and memory overhead of the full pipeline is not reported, and the 'practical for local inference' claim is not substantiated by timing measurements.

The theoretical framing is thin. The 'hill climbing' interpretation is informal; the empirical justification for restricting exploration to the first λ=15 of 50 steps rests on a single hand-wavy observation (a DDIM coefficient 'above 0.02'), and there is no analysis of when the inversion operator Ψ, which does not correspond to a valid reverse-process transition, preserves sample quality or induces distributional bias.

Statistical rigor is lacking. No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for any comparison, and several of the decisive margins (e.g., 0.2678 vs. 0.2671 HPSv2) are small enough to plausibly be noise given 500/200 prompts.

Some ablation results are internally inconsistent or anomalous (e.g., AES-as-reward yielding the best AES score of 5.783 while degrading other metrics, and ablation numbers that do not align with the main-table configuration), and the ablations use different settings (Nb=1, δ=0) from the main experiments, making cross-referencing difficult.

The claim of 'substantially improves generation quality' is overstated relative to the evidence: improvements over the strongest baseline (SOP) are modest on preference-based metrics, negligible on AES for alignment-focused setups, and concentrated on the self-reward metric.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: viewing conditional diffusion sampling as a hill-climbing process prone to reward/alignment plateaus, and connecting this to limitations of CFG, resampling, and recent test-time scaling methods.

The adaptive inversion depth is a sensible and practically useful mechanism: increasing rollback strength (Δ) only when shallow perturbations fail is a natural improvement over fixed-depth resampling/search approaches, and is intuitively illustrated in Figure 1 and formalized in Algorithm 1.

Thorough ablation studies covering reward model choice (Table 2), exploration initiation criteria (Always/Random/Reward-Based), max inversion depth and acceptance threshold (Figure 2), and exploration window — giving useful guidance on compute/quality trade-offs (25.8× vs 8.6× vs 3.2× NFEs).

Consistent quantitative gains over DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP on two standard benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench) across four human-aligned metrics, with a lower average NFE overhead than SOP (7.6× vs 10×), plus supporting qualitative comparisons.
The method is training-free and plug-in style, requiring only an external reward model, which makes it broadly applicable to existing diffusion pipelines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to concurrent/related work. The method is essentially a combination of existing ingredients: reward-guided rejection, random noise injection/backward resampling (RePaint, Restart, Z-Sampling), and greedy path search (SOP). The main new element — progressively deeper inversion upon stagnation — is an incremental extension. The 'hill-climbing' framing is presented as a contribution but is largely conceptual rather than developed into analysis.

Restricted experimental scope undermines the 'model-agnostic' and 'broadly applicable' claims: all experiments use only Stable Diffusion 2.1 (base) with T=50, CFG=5.5 on two text-to-image benchmarks. No results on SDXL, other solvers, or other modalities (video, etc.) despite the abstract's generality claims.

Reward model (ImageReward) is both the search signal and one of the reported metrics, creating a reward-optimization confound. Gains on the non-reward metrics are real but small (e.g., HPSv2 0.2678 vs SOP's 0.2671 on Pick-a-Pic). A human evaluation study is absent, which would be the most convincing evidence for perceptual claims.

The efficiency comparison with SOP is arguably not apples-to-apples: SOP's candidate count is tuned (5) to match NFEs, and the NFE accounting does not appear to include the reward model forward passes, which are a non-trivial extra cost of the approach.

Restricting exploration to the first λ=15 steps is justified heuristically via the magnitude of the clean-image weight, but misalignment traps can also arise at later timesteps; no analysis or experiment addresses this limitation or the risk of diversity collapse / mode narrowing from repeated reward-greedy acceptance.

No theoretical treatment of when the adaptive retreat improves over baselines, no variance/significance reporting on benchmark results, and no mention of code release, which limits reproducibility of the many hyperparameters (δ, λ, dmax, N, Nb, batched search schedule).

strengths: The proposed Ctrl-Z Sampling is a simple, well-motivated inference-time strategy: reward-guided detection of stagnation followed by noise inversion with progressively increasing depth, forming an adaptive hill-climbing search. The algorithm (Alg. 1) is clearly specified and reproducible, and the method is model-agnostic.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: two diffusion backbones (U-Net-based SD 2.1 and Transformer-based Hunyuan-DiT), three benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, T2I-CompBench), four evaluation metrics, and multiple baselines (DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, SOP) under comparable NFE budgets.

The ablation studies are a highlight: the paper systematically examines search depth vs. candidate width (Fig. 2), choice of reward model (Tab. 3), exploration initiation strategies (Always/Random/Reward-based, Tabs. 3, 5, 6), acceptance threshold δ (Fig. 4), and exploration window λ (Tab. 7). The finding that deeper but sparser exploration outperforms wider-but-shallow search under matched budgets is an interesting and useful insight.

The paper is transparent about limitations (fixed acceptance threshold, restricted exploration window, incomplete scaling validation) and honestly discusses cases where the method underperforms (e.g., numeracy with Hunyuan-DiT, AES insensitivity), including a plausible analysis of reward over-optimization with the 'Always' strategy.
Computational overhead (~7-9× NFEs) is moderate relative to related test-time scaling approaches, and candidate evaluation is parallelizable.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a combination of known ingredients—DDIM resampling/inversion (Lugmayr et al., Restart Sampling), reward-guided best-of-N selection (SOP, particle-based search), and a greedy hill-climbing acceptance rule. The main new element is the adaptive inversion depth, which is a fairly natural incremental extension. The contribution type appears to be Algorithms/General, and under this framing the technical advance is modest relative to SOP and Z-Sampling.

Evidence of possible reward hacking: the largest and most consistent gains appear on ImageReward—the very reward model guiding exploration (e.g., IR 0.194→1.138 on SD2.1, ~6×)—while gains on held-out metrics are much smaller (HPSv2 +0.11 to +0.4) and PickScore is sometimes below SOP (21.02 vs 21.12 on Pick-a-Pic SD2.1). No FID/precision-recall, user study, or other reward-independent human evaluation is provided to confirm genuine quality improvement rather than metric over-optimization.

The improvements on non-reward metrics are small and the paper reports no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance; given stochastic exploration and random noise seeds, the practical significance of ~0.1-point HPSv2 differences is unclear.

Evaluation is confined to relatively dated models (SD 2.1 base, Hunyuan-DiT); no experiments on stronger modern models (SDXL, Flux), which would strengthen claims of practical relevance and generality.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness that undermine polish: the abstract claims '6.72×' NFE increase while the text reports 7-9×; SOP is attributed to Ma et al. 2025 in the main text but to Kim, Kim, and Park 2025 in the supplementary; SD 2.1 is cited to 'Feng et al. 2023' (incorrect attribution); naming alternates between 'Hunyuan-DiT' and 'Hy-DiT'.

Key design choices rest on heuristics rather than analysis: the hill-climbing framing is intuitive but no quantitative evidence is given that diffusion sampling actually gets trapped in 'local maxima' (e.g., reward-trajectory statistics); the restriction to the first λ steps is justified only by a weight-magnitude observation; the detection criterion (Eq. 6) reduces to 'reward decreased since last accepted state', which is a weak notion of a local maximum.

The claimed efficiency advantage over SOP rests on a 7.72 vs 9 NFE comparison; a matched-NFE comparison at identical budgets, or SOP with more/fewer candidates, would make the efficiency claims more convincing.

strengths: The method is training-free, model-agnostic, and cleanly presented; the 'adaptive inversion depth' idea (deepening exploration only when shallow perturbations fail) is a sensible and clearly motivated extension of existing rollback/resampling strategies.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: two architectures (SD 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT) across three benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, T2I-CompBench), with multiple human-aligned metrics and reasonably fair NFE-matched comparisons against SOP, Z-Sampling, Resampling, and DDIM.

The ablation study is thorough and honest: reward-model choice, exploration initiation criteria (Always/Random/Reward-based), exploration window λ, depth dmax, candidate width N, and threshold δ are all examined, and budget-controlled comparisons (Tables 5-6) are a nice touch.
The limitations section is substantive and candid (fixed per-step threshold δ, restricted evaluation scale), and the paper acknowledges the risk of reward over-optimization.
The approach is parallelizable across candidates, and the supplementary gives enough implementation detail (hardware, versions, hyperparameters) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially SOP/Resampling-style backward rollback augmented with (a) an adaptively increasing inversion depth and (b) a reward-based trigger. Both ingredients are natural, incremental refinements of closely related test-time scaling work (Ma et al. 2025; Bai et al. 2024; Lugmayr et al. 2022); the 'hill-climbing' framing is intuitive but not a formal contribution.

Gains over the strongest baseline are marginal. On SD2.1/Pick-a-Pic, Ctrl-Z is essentially tied with SOP (HPSv2 27.34 vs 27.23; PickScore 21.02 vs 21.12 — actually worse on PickScore); DrawBench differences are within noise. Only ImageReward improves noticeably, and ImageReward is exactly the model used to guide exploration, raising a metric-circularity / reward-hacking concern that is discussed but not resolved (e.g., no human evaluation).

The 'only 6.72x NFE' framing in the abstract is misleading: 6-9x more function evaluations is a substantial compute increase for gains that are small on non-reward metrics; comparison against cheap baselines like CFG amplification or best-of-N at matched NFE is absent.

Algorithmic sloppiness: in Algorithm 1, the acceptance check at line 27 tests rcand (the last sampled candidate) rather than best_score, and the break condition can diverge from the best-state bookkeeping; also there are typos ('We the propose', 'otherwise scheming progressively deeper explorations') that suggest insufficient polish.

Evaluation is restricted to older/relatively small models (SD 2.1, Hunyuan-DiT) at 50 steps; no evidence on modern, stronger generators (SDXL, FLUX, etc.) where local-optimum escape may behave very differently, and the authors themselves concede the inference-scaling story is not validated at larger budgets.

The inversion operator (Eq. 5) is just standard DDIM forward noising with fresh Gaussian noise, so 'controlled inversion' oversells a simple renoising step; no theoretical or empirical analysis (e.g., of when deeper rollback actually helps, or of the stochasticity/acceptance trade-off) is provided.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the numerous tuned hyperparameters (λ, dmax, N, δ, CFG=5.5).

strengths: The method is simple, model-agnostic, and clearly described, with a complete algorithm (Alg. 1) and a reasonable motivation framed around escaping local maxima during deterministic DDIM sampling.

Experiments cover two architecturally different diffusion backbones (U-Net-based SD 2.1 and Transformer-based Hunyuan-DiT), three established benchmarks (Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, T2I-CompBench), and four evaluation metrics, providing cross-architecture evidence of generality.

Ablations are unusually thorough: reward model choice, exploration initiation criteria (Always/Random/Reward-based) under budget-matched comparisons, inversion depth dmax vs. candidate width N, acceptance threshold δ, and exploration window λ are all examined, and the discussion of trade-offs (e.g., reward over-optimization in late-stage exploration) is thoughtful.

The paper is honest about limitations, including the fixed acceptance threshold, potential reward over-fitting, and restricted evaluation scale, and it discusses societal/quality trade-offs (e.g., AES improvements) rather than only optimizing the guiding reward.

The claimed NFE cost (~7-9x) is moderate relative to broader test-time scaling methods, and the observation that adaptive depth can substitute for candidate width is a useful empirical insight for budget-constrained inference.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core mechanism—reverting to a noisier state, perturbing, denoising forward, and accepting based on a reward model—is very close to existing approaches (Resampling, Z-Sampling, Restart Sampling, SOP, and other 2025 test-time search works). The main new element is the adaptive (increasing) inversion depth triggered by reward stagnation, which is a modest heuristic extension rather than a new algorithmic framework.

Gains over the strongest baseline (SOP) are small and mixed: e.g., on SD 2.1 Pick-a-Pic, Ctrl-Z slightly exceeds SOP on IR/HPS but is slightly below on PickScore; AES differences are marginal. No variance estimates, seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for any comparison, so the claimed improvements may not be robust.

Potential reward hacking is a central concern: ImageReward is used both to guide exploration and as an evaluation metric, and the large IR gains likely overstate true quality. There is no human evaluation or MLLM-based assessment to substantiate alignment claims beyond learned preference metrics.

The inversion operator (Eq. 5) injects fresh random noise rather than performing a principled DDIM inversion, so the claim that previously accumulated semantic structure is 'retained' is only loosely supported; the effect is essentially restarting from a partially corrupted latent, and a more careful theoretical or empirical characterization is missing.

Algorithm 1 contains an apparent implementation ambiguity: the break condition at line 27 uses r_cand from the final loop iteration rather than best_score, which could discard a valid improving candidate found at an earlier noise draw; the detection criterion in Eq. 6 (reward below previous best) also does not fully match the 'stagnation' description.

Evaluation is limited to somewhat dated models (SD 2.1 base, Hunyuan-DiT) at 50 steps; results on modern high-quality models (e.g., SDXL, Flux) where failure modes may differ are absent, and large-scale behavior is explicitly deferred to future work.

The 'hill climbing' interpretation is purely an analogy with no formal analysis (e.g., when the reward-stagnation trigger actually corresponds to a local optimum, or convergence properties of the zigzag search), which weakens the conceptual contribution.

The efficiency claim relative to SOP depends on approximate NFE matching across configurations (7.72 vs. 9.0), and the budget-controlled 'Always' ablation shows some metrics favor more frequent exploration, so the practical superiority of the reward-based trigger over simpler random triggering is not decisively established.
